title: Multiculturalism

cards.b:
Almost every state is culturally plural. Multiculturalism asks how a liberal state should treat minority languages, religions and ways of life. Should it be 'blind' to difference, or recognise it?

This is a Paper I favourite because it links liberalism, rights, the communitarian critique and Indian secularism.

Classic liberalism offers equal individual rights and neutrality. Multiculturalists say neutrality is a myth: public holidays, language and school curricula usually reflect the majority culture.

So minorities need recognition and sometimes special measures. The aim is equal respect and a fair chance to keep one's culture, not separatism.

Will Kymlicka, Multicultural Citizenship (1995), argues from liberal premises. Culture is the 'context of choice' that gives individuals meaning, so protecting it protects autonomy.

He lists three kinds of group rights: self-government rights (national minorities), polyethnic rights (immigrants: exemptions, funding), special representation rights. He separates external protections (acceptable) from internal restrictions on members (not acceptable).

Charles Taylor, Multiculturalism and the Politics of Recognition (1992). Identity is formed through recognition by others. Misrecognition can harm like oppression.

Taylor, a communitarian, distinguishes the politics of universalism (same rights for all) from the politics of difference. His example is Quebec's French-language policy.

Bhikhu Parekh, Rethinking Multiculturalism (2000), proposes intercultural dialogue: no culture is perfect, so each should be open to criticism by others. He denies that liberalism is the only standard.

Iris Marion Young pushes for group representation for oppressed groups, in Justice and the Politics of Difference (1990).
Kymlicka tries to bridge the two, while Barry and Okin attack multiculturalism from within liberalism.

• Brian Barry, Culture and Equality (2001): group exemptions break equal citizenship.
  • Susan Okin, 'Is Multiculturalism Bad for Women?' (1999): protecting a culture may protect patriarchy.
  • It can freeze cultures and ignore internal diversity.
  • Conservatives say it weakens national unity. The leaders of Germany, Britain and France declared multiculturalism a failure in 2010-11.

States handle diversity differently.

  • Assimilation: minorities adopt the dominant culture (France's laicite).
  • Integration: common civic rules, room for difference.
  • Multiculturalism: official support for cultural diversity (Canada, since 1971).

Canada's Multiculturalism Act (1988) is the standard example.

Keep the name, the year and the one-line claim ready. These three details are what examiners look for when they check a concept.

India has long practised group-differentiated rights: Articles 25-30 (religious freedom, cultural and educational rights of minorities, Art. 29-30), Schedules Five and Six, linguistic states, reservations and personal laws.

Rajeev Bhargava calls this contextual secularism, with principled distance and not strict separation. The Shah Bano case (1985) and the Uniform Civil Code debate (Art. 44) show the Okin-style tension between group rights and gender equality.

"Examine the case for group-differentiated rights in a liberal democracy."
"Is multiculturalism compatible with gender justice?"
"Evaluate Kymlicka's views on minority rights."
"How does the Indian Constitution reflect a multicultural approach?"

Structure: liberal neutrality, then Kymlicka and Taylor, Parekh, critiques from Barry and Okin, then India (Arts. 25-30, UCC debate).
